title: Food-Sharing Apps: More Than a Cheap Meal

paragraphs.text: At the end of the day, many bakeries and restaurants still have food that has not been sold. Preparing exactly the right amount is difficult because the number of customers can change from one day to the next. As a result, food that is still perfectly good may be thrown away. Food-sharing apps offer businesses another option: selling their remaining food at a lower price instead of putting it in the rubbish. The aim is to find customers for food that would otherwise be wasted.

The process is fairly simple. A business puts an offer on the app, showing the price and the time when the food can be collected. A customer reserves an order and pays for it through the app. Later, the customer visits the business during the collection period. In some cases, the food is sold in a surprise bag, so customers cannot choose exactly what they will receive. Businesses should still provide information about ingredients that may cause allergic reactions. A surprise about the contents should not become a risk to someone's health.

Both businesses and customers can benefit from this arrangement. Customers receive food for less than its usual price, while businesses earn some money from products that might otherwise bring them no income. Businesses may also spend less on removing rubbish. However, the lower prices are not meant to replace normal sales. Offers usually become available only when a business knows that it has more food than it can sell that day. This helps keep the focus on reducing waste rather than producing extra food for the app.

Although the idea sounds convenient, it does not suit everyone. Some people cannot reach a shop during its short collection period, especially if they work late or depend on public transport. Others need to plan meals carefully and cannot use a surprise bag. For these customers, useful information matters as much as a low price. A clear description of the offer and realistic collection times can help them decide whether an order meets their needs before they pay.

These apps are therefore only one part of the solution to food waste. Businesses also need to understand why food remains unsold. Keeping records of what is left each day can help them estimate how much to prepare in future. Selling leftover food is useful, but preventing large amounts of it from being left over is better. The most successful approach combines a way to share remaining food with careful planning before the food is made.

questions.stem: What do we learn from paragraph I? Choose TWO correct answers.
questions.feedback_en: Use the evidence in the indicated paragraph and check the exact task.

options.A: Why businesses may have food left at the end of the day.
options.B: When the first food-sharing app was developed.
options.C: Why customers prefer bakeries to restaurants.
options.D: How apps offer an alternative to throwing away good food.
options.E: Which businesses waste the largest amounts of food.
options.F: Why all food left at closing time is unsafe to eat.

B.error_description_en: The paragraph gives no date or history of the apps.

C.error_description_en: Bakeries and restaurants are examples; customer preferences are not compared.

E.error_description_en: No comparison of the amounts wasted by different businesses is given.

F.error_description_en: The paragraph says that the food may still be perfectly good.
